blocks.x: It's fair to say I was pretty taken by the G Pro X2 Superstrike when Logitech launched it earlier this year. It was the first mouse I'd seen in a long time that did something genuinely revolutionary. But, just seven months later, it is being rendered all but obsolete by the new G Pro X3 Superstrike.

The revolutionary part of the original was that it made its switches analogue and paired this with haptic feedback to replicate the feeling of a click. This allows for adjustable actuation, meaning you can set it low for less time between deciding to click and actually clicking, and the haptics make sure you feel the click exactly when you should, whenever it's set to actuate.

That being said, it's far from a perfect mouse. I was thoroughly enamoured by it during my testing, and I still think it deserves a heck of a lot of credit for that revolutionary tech alone. But over time its flaws have come to feel more pronounced to me.

It's pretty much the same as the Superlight 2 in other respects, from the shape to the weight, side buttons, and scroll wheel. The side buttons are pretty mushy, the scroll wheel has problems with long-presses, and most importantly—and specifically in the case of the original Superstrike, not the Superlight 2—it's quite top-heavy thanks to those new internals.

The worst problem for a lot of people was that front-heavy weighting, as that can cause drag and, well, just not feel very smooth when picking up and moving the mouse. Given it's such an expensive mouse and is aimed squarely at competitive gamers who need great balance and weighting, and although it hasn't bothered me too much, this has been a big issue for many.

So, these seven months later, stepping up to the plate is the X3 Superstrike, which fixes this weighting issue and has a couple of other benefits, but it makes me wonder why Logitech didn't just wait and release this version in the first place.

Sensor: Hero 2, 48K DPI
Battery life: 135 hours
Weight: 57 g (59 g in Europe)
Colours: Midnight Black or Magenta Eclipse (pink and black)
Price: $200

It's basically the same weight, with a couple of grams shaved off only if you're outside of Europe, but battery life has been improved by 50% up to 135 hours at 1 kHz polling, assuming you're clicking just shy of once per second. It's also got a slightly upgraded sensor, with a bump to DPI, acceleration, and max speed—but nothing major.

In terms of what it actually feels like to use, it feels almost exactly the same as the original X2 Superstrike—except the weighting is more balanced. I've been using it for the past few days and most of the time I forget I'm not just using the X2 Superstrike. Occasionally I'm reminded of the better balance, but apart from that both feel about the same to use, whether for work or gaming.

You do get different colour choices with the X3, though: Midnight Black or Magenta Eclipse (pink and black). I'm not sure why the original white-and-black combo isn't available for the X3, but the black version I have under my palm looks good enough to me.
In other words, just seven months after the X2's launch, the X3 launches—for an extra $20 at $200/€190, mind you—and very much feels like the X2, but improved in a couple of simple ways.

It's fair to say I was pretty taken by the G Pro X2 Superstrike when Logitech launched it earlier this year. It was the first mouse I'd seen in a long time that did something genuinely revolutionary. But, just seven months later, it is being rendered all but obsolete by the new G Pro X3 Superstrike.

The revolutionary part of the original was that it made its switches analogue and paired this with haptic feedback to replicate the feeling of a click. This allows for adjustable actuation, meaning you can set it low for less time between deciding to click and actually clicking, and the haptics make sure you feel the click exactly when you should, whenever it's set to actuate.

That being said, it's far from a perfect mouse. I was thoroughly enamoured by it during my testing, and I still think it deserves a heck of a lot of credit for that revolutionary tech alone. But over time its flaws have come to feel more pronounced to me.

It's pretty much the same as the Superlight 2 in other respects, from the shape to the weight, side buttons, and scroll wheel. The side buttons are pretty mushy, the scroll wheel has problems with long-presses, and most importantly—and specifically in the case of the original Superstrike, not the Superlight 2—it's quite top-heavy thanks to those new internals.

The worst problem for a lot of people was that front-heavy weighting, as that can cause drag and, well, just not feel very smooth when picking up and moving the mouse. Given it's such an expensive mouse and is aimed squarely at competitive gamers who need great balance and weighting, and although it hasn't bothered me too much, this has been a big issue for many.

So, these seven months later, stepping up to the plate is the X3 Superstrike, which fixes this weighting issue and has a couple of other benefits, but it makes me wonder why Logitech didn't just wait and release this version in the first place.

X2 Superstrike

Sensor: Hero 2, 44K DPI
Battery life: 90 hours
Weight: 59 g
Colours: White with black buttons
Price: $180

X3 Superstrike

Sensor: Hero 2, 48K DPI
Battery life: 135 hours
Weight: 57 g (59 g in Europe)
Colours: Midnight Black or Magenta Eclipse (pink and black)
Price: $200

It's basically the same weight, with a couple of grams shaved off only if you're outside of Europe, but battery life has been improved by 50% up to 135 hours at 1 kHz polling, assuming you're clicking just shy of once per second. It's also got a slightly upgraded sensor, with a bump to DPI, acceleration, and max speed—but nothing major.

In terms of what it actually feels like to use, it feels almost exactly the same as the original X2 Superstrike—except the weighting is more balanced. I've been using it for the past few days and most of the time I forget I'm not just using the X2 Superstrike. Occasionally I'm reminded of the better balance, but apart from that both feel about the same to use, whether for work or gaming.

You do get different colour choices with the X3, though: Midnight Black or Magenta Eclipse (pink and black). I'm not sure why the original white-and-black combo isn't available for the X3, but the black version I have under my palm looks good enough to me.

In other words, just seven months after the X2's launch, the X3 launches—for an extra $20 at $200/€190, mind you—and very much feels like the X2, but improved in a couple of simple ways.
